pulls.title: Fixes from the pre-submission cold read
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Fixes from the pre-submission cold read (a working-group reviewer and an implementer persona), with one commit per finding so any of them can be dropped on its own. Every dependency claim was checked against the cached RFC and draft text.

## Corrections (no design change)

| Commit | Finding |
|---|---|
| Limit client processing of the response to JWT authorization grants | 3.6 applied to every token, so a client discarded a valid DPoP-bound access token from a server without the `cnf` parameter, contradicting RFC 9449 §5. Access tokens now follow `token_type`. |
| State when Token Exchange issues a JWT authorization grant | A grant is a JWT whose `aud` identifies an authorization server. |
| Require the binding determination for every audience of a grant | RFC 10070 allows several `aud` values. |
| Require a cnf claim when the response carries the cnf parameter | A readable grant without a `cnf` claim passed every client check. |
| Order DPoP proof validation before grant validation | Fixes error precedence (`use_dpop_nonce`, `invalid_dpop_proof`, `invalid_grant`), and an invalid DPoP proof is rejected whatever the grant's binding (RFC 9449 §5). |
| Clarify invalid_client precedence and the scope of the reuse rule | A grant that fails validation is not bound; the not-recorded-as-used rule covers every grant. |
| Say how an audience maps to the requesting client | An access token's `aud` usually holds resource identifiers. |
| Require client identification for per-client enforcement | The `grant_types` limit cannot apply to a request that identifies no client. |
| Narrow what advertising jwt-dpop shows | Deployments of JWT-DPOP-GRANT advertise the same URN; what both guarantee is `jkt` verification. Open issue 4 reworded. |
| List remaining differences from JWT-DPOP-GRANT and ID-JAG | `invalid_grant` instead of `invalid_dpop_proof` for a missing proof. ID-JAG §4.4 uses `jwt-dpop` for DPoP-bound grants, which Appendix A item 2 denied. |
| Simplify the refresh verification and metadata mapping passages | Two of the passages the reviewer found hardest to read. |
| Move the IANA registry reference to informative references | Clears the idnits3 comment. |

## Design changes (each recommended by both reviewers)

| Commit | Change and reason |
|---|---|
| Issue an unbound grant when the issuer cannot bind it | Resolves open issue 2. Rejecting with `invalid_target` meant a client holding a DPoP-bound subject token could get no grant for an audience that does not verify bindings, which breaks identity chaining as soon as one domain adopts this, and broke SDKs that send DPoP on every request. A client that requires a bound grant still discards an unbound one. `invalid_target` remains for a profile that requires binding. Adds a third ID-JAG conflict (§9.11.1.1). |
| Accept the jwk confirmation member at redemption | The "member the profile defines" clause had no binding or refresh rules. A `jwk` member is verified by thumbprint, like `jkt`. Issuers still emit `jkt` or `x5t#S256`. |
| Allow the grant's certificate for a certificate-bound grant with a DPoP proof | Both bindings are safe; keeps mTLS-only resource servers working and removes a conflict with ID-JAG §9.11.2.2. Notes ID-CHAINING Appendix B.3. |
| Let a refresh token be bound to a client that the grant identifies | Restores credential rotation for confidential clients (RFC 9449 §5). The replay that motivated key binding needs an attacker authenticating as its own client, which a check that the grant identifies the authenticated client defeats (ID-JAG §4.4.1 already does it). |

## Checks

- Builds after every commit; `make`, `make lint` and the versioned `-00` build pass; no artwork line over 72 columns.
- BCP 14 keywords go from 45 to 46: the `invalid_target` MUST in 3.4 and the retry MAY in 3.6 are removed, 3.1's bind-or-unbound rule replaces two keywords with four, and the refresh-token exception adds a MAY.

## Not in this PR

- Renaming `jwt-dpop` to a method-neutral `jwt-pop` with a confirmation-method metadata parameter (open issues 1 and 4). Pending a decision.
- Section 1.1 says this draft replaces JWT-DPOP-GRANT. That needs its author's agreement before submission.

pulls.title: Replace jwt-dpop with method-neutral jwt-pop and confirmation-method discovery
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Replaces the DPoP-only `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-dpop` grant type with a method-neutral `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-pop`, and adds explicit discovery of the confirmation methods a consuming authorization server verifies (`jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported`). Kept separate from #1 so the protocol change can be reviewed on its own.

## Why

A separate grant type is what lets a consuming server say "bound grants only" through existing `grant_types` registration (§6.2). A server can already refuse unbound grants by policy while accepting `jwt-bearer`, but `grant_types` cannot express it. That reason applies to certificate-bound grants as much as DPoP-bound ones, and the `cnf` member already selects the verification procedure, so method-specific grant types add little. A method-neutral grant type no longer tells an issuer which method a server verifies, so discovery changes with it.

Resolves open issue 1 and the server-discovery part of open issue 4. Client opt-in to certificate binding stays open (open issue 3, reframed).

## Requirements this meets

| Requirement | Where |
|---|---|
| A server advertising `jwt-pop` publishes a nonempty `jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported` (RECOMMENDED; REQUIRED with `jwt-pop`), whose values are Confirmation Method Values from the RFC 7800 registry (`jkt`, `jwk`, `x5t#S256`), applying whatever the grant type or the grant's profile; `jkt` does not imply `jwk` | §6.1 |
| `jwt-pop` alone is no evidence for any method; missing metadata is no evidence, while configuration or an established trust relationship still is | §6.1, §3.4 |
| Enforcement stays independent of the grant type: a bound grant sent with `jwt-bearer` is still verified | §4.2 (unchanged), §8.2 |
| `jwt-dpop` kept for existing clients with its `jkt` requirement, stated in this document and registered as a legacy URN; servers SHOULD keep supporting and advertising it while clients rely on it; clients use it at servers that advertise only `jwt-dpop` | §4.1, §4.1.2, §10 |
| Supporting both URNs does not authorize every client for both; new clients use `jwt-pop` | §6.2 |
| The `jwt-pop` preference is conditioned on the client's registration, and the legacy route is listed | §4.1 |
| The request-level purpose is explicit: `jwt-pop` requires a bound grant in each request and fails closed (`unsupported_grant_type`), unlike client metadata, which is ignored when unknown | §6.2, §8.2 |
| `jwt-pop` has no corresponding `response_types` value (RFC 7591 §2.1) | §6.2 |
| IANA: `jwt-pop` and the legacy `jwt-dpop` in the OAuth URI registry (JWT-DPOP-GRANT, which requested `jwt-dpop`, is replaced), and `jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported` in the OAuth Authorization Server Metadata registry | §10 |
| Matching ID-JAG change proposed (§4.4 and §8 use `jwt-pop`) | Appendix A |
| Coordination with the JWT-DPOP-GRANT authors on replacement and compatibility | Open issue 4 |

## Design considered and reverted

Commits 6 and 7 replaced the dedicated parameter with one grant-profile URN per method (`urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-profile:pop-jkt`, `pop-jwk`, `pop-x5t-s256`) in ID-JAG's `authorization_grant_profiles_supported`, for both server and client metadata. On review they are reverted (commits 8 and 9):

- A `pop-*` entry names a proof capability, not a grant profile, so one list would mix two kinds of entry, and implementers would map three URNs back to confirmation-member names.
- The client-side signal was really an issuance-policy opt-in ("bind my grants to the certificate I present"), not a capability: a client can support certificate-bound grants and still reserve its issuer-facing certificate. That was the main gain from the reuse.
- It made the generic mechanism depend normatively on ID-JAG.

Open issue 3 now asks whether a client metadata parameter should express opt-in to certificate binding, and records the profiles parameter as one possible carrier. The history keeps both designs for the working group.

## Commits

1. Replace jwt-dpop with jwt-pop and advertise verified confirmation methods
2. Keep jwt-dpop for existing clients with its published jkt requirement
3. Update the appendices, open issues and history for jwt-pop
4. Condition the jwt-pop preference on the client's registration
5. State that jwt-pop has no corresponding response type
6. Advertise confirmation methods with authorization_grant_profiles_supported
7. Define the certificate capability independently of client authentication
8. Revert of 7
9. Revert of 6
10. Scope method discovery across profiles and reframe certificate opt-in
11. Explain the request-level purpose of jwt-pop
12. Register jwt-dpop and state the legacy rules in this document
13. Direct clients to jwt-dpop at servers that implement only JWT-DPOP-GRANT
14. Keep jwt-dpop supported and advertised where clients rely on it
15. Define the values and requirement level of jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported
16. Answer the revised profile item for ID-JAG and cover 4.1.2 in 6.2
17. Record the client-metadata alternative to jwt-pop as an open issue (open issue 5)
18. Apply the registration check to the jwt-dpop preference
19. Describe the metadata alternative's cost as confirming the registration

Commits 11–17 come from a fresh-eyes review and an external review of commit 10, and 18–19 from a further external review; none found a security issue.

## Checks

- Builds after every commit; 37 pages; no artwork line over 72 columns.
- BCP 14 keywords go from 46 to 52: the metadata parameter (OPTIONAL, SHOULD publish), the `jwt-pop` advertisement (SHOULD) with its nonempty-list MUST, issuer reliance on listed members (MAY), legacy support (MAY) with its `jkt` MUST, and `jwt-dpop` as `jkt` evidence (MAY), replacing the old `jwt-dpop` advertisement SHOULD and reliance MAY. The requirement set after commit 10 is identical to that after commit 5. Commits 11–17 bring the count to 54: the parameter becomes RECOMMENDED/REQUIRED (replacing a SHOULD, OPTIONAL and conditional MUST), and three SHOULDs are added for legacy support, legacy advertisement, and client use of `jwt-dpop` at legacy-only servers.

## Before submission

The IANA registry lists neither URN, which supports doing this now, but that does not show that no `jwt-dpop` implementations exist; implementation evidence should decide how much of §4.1.2 is needed. The replacement and compatibility language needs agreement from the JWT-DPOP-GRANT authors.

pulls.title: Align document structure with OAuth RFC conventions
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Structural pass aligning the draft with the RFCs it models (RFC 9449, 8705, 8693, 7523). No requirement is intended to change. Three structural commits and one scope fix, reviewable separately.

## New outline

```
1  Introduction (1.1 Relationship to Other Documents, 1.2 Conventions and Terminology)
2  Protocol Overview
3  Bound JWT Authorization Grants
   3.1 Confirmation Claim  3.2 Comparing Confirmation Values
4  Issuing a Bound Grant
   4.1 Token Exchange Request                         (client)
   4.2 Issuing Authorization Server Processing        (issuing authorization server)
       4.2.1 DPoP Binding  4.2.2 Certificate Binding
       4.2.3 Bound Subject and Actor Tokens  4.2.4 Binding the Grant
   4.3 Token Exchange Response                        (issuing authorization server)
   4.4 Client Processing of the Response              (client)
   4.5 Other Issuance Interfaces
5  Redeeming a Bound Grant
   5.1 Access Token Request (5.1.1 jwt-pop, 5.1.2 legacy jwt-dpop)   (client)
   5.2 Resource Authorization Server Processing       (resource authorization server)
   5.3 Access Token Response  5.4 Refresh Tokens
   5.5 Bound Grant in Place of Client Authentication
6  Error Responses  7  Metadata  8  Profiling This Specification
9  Security Considerations (enforcement, replay, client identity, issuance)
10 Privacy  11 IANA  Appendix A Profiles  Appendix B Open Issues
```

## Commits

1. **Split Sections 3 and 4 by role; bullets and a table in Section 1.** Request / issuer processing / response / client processing, as in RFC 8693 §2 and RFC 9126 §2. DPoP Binding now sits beside Certificate Binding. Client-side sentences and the example request move out of the server subsections. §1.1 is one bullet per related document, and the grant type short names are a table.
2. **Rename "consuming authorization server" to "resource authorization server".** It matches ID-JAG's role name. The role definitions point at the matching ID-JAG roles. "Issuing authorization server" is kept because the identity-chaining issuer is not necessarily an IdP.
3. **Give the grant format its own section; order Security Considerations.** The `cnf` claim format and Comparing Confirmation Values move into a new Section 3, before the protocol, as RFC 9449 §4 and RFC 7523 §3 define their artifacts first. Section 4 is retitled "Issuing a Bound Grant", since 4.5 covers other interfaces and its child "Token Exchange Request" no longer repeats the parent. The security subsections are grouped by lifecycle.
4. **Restore the request-specific key selection in Binding the Grant.** A scope fix to commit 3, from review; see the scope table.

## Evidence

| Commit | BCP 14 sentences (order, added, removed) | Figure contents | Build |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Same keyword sequence (53). One reworded: "MUST validate the DPoP proof" becomes "…the DPoP proof of a binding request", restoring the scope its old heading supplied. One keyword-free error mapping (§1.1, `invalid_grant` instead of `invalid_dpop_proof`) became a sub-bullet. | identical | ok |
| 2 | Identical once the rename is neutralized | one figure changed: the diagram's "Consuming" box label | ok |
| 3 | Identical | identical (positions only) | ok |
| 4 | Identical (one keyword-free sentence reworded) | identical | ok |

Overall, the draft still builds at 38 pages with no artwork line over 72 columns. Citations resolve; the checker's "unresolved" list contains only figure and table anchors, which it does not recognize, and the build resolves them.

## Scope review of moved text

Matching counts do not show that a moved sentence still covers what it covered. Each requirement-bearing or definitional move was checked:

| Text | From → to | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Subject and actor tokens not treated as used on rejection (MUST NOT) | §3 intro → §4.2 intro | The sentence scopes itself ("When it rejects a request for a JWT authorization grant"). Unchanged. |
| DPoP proof validation (MUST) | §3.1 Binding Request → §4.2.1 DPoP Binding | The old heading implied "of a binding request"; that phrase is now in the sentence. |
| Bind, unbound or reject (MUSTs) | §3.1 → §4.2.1 | The sentence scopes itself ("In response to a binding request…"). Unchanged. |
| "binds a grant only as described in §3.1 and this section" | §3.2 → §4.2 intro, as "only as described in this section" | §4.2 adds 4.2.3 and 4.2.4, which constrain binding without adding ways to bind. Equivalent. |
| "A TLS client certificate is not a binding request" | §3.2 → §4.1 | Definitional; it introduces the term on the client side. Unchanged. |
| Exactly one confirmation member | issuer's "To bind a grant…" → §3.1 | Kept as an issuer rule ("An issuing authorization server binds a grant by including … exactly one"), with a pointer to the resource authorization server's rejection in §5.2. An intermediate version read "A bound grant is a JWT authorization grant whose `cnf` claim contains exactly one confirmation member". That redefined the term against §1.2 and the §5.2 check, and was corrected before this commit. |
| Which key or certificate the issuer binds to | issuer's format bullets ("which for a binding request is the key in the `jwk` JOSE Header Parameter of the DPoP proof"; "which for a Token Exchange request is the TLS client certificate") → §4.2.4 | Commit 3 dropped both conditions, so §4.5, which applies §4.2.4 to other issuance interfaces, would have required a DPoP proof from an interface with its own proof-of-possession mechanism. Commit 4 restores them: "For a binding request, that key is…; for a Token Exchange request bound to a certificate, that certificate is…". Found in review; the unchanged keyword sequence did not show it. |
| Client proves possession of a bound subject token | new descriptive sentence in §4.1 | Now ends "unless §4.2.3 exempts it", so it does not contradict the authenticated-audience exemption. |
| Comparing Confirmation Values; Security subsections | moved | Text unchanged; references unchanged. |

## Terminology

§5.2's actor is the resource authorization server. "Resource server" now appears only in its RFC 8693 §2.3 sense: a resource server acting as a Token Exchange client and exchanging an access token it received (§4.2.3, twice).

## Not in this PR

An Implementation Considerations section (RFC 8705 §6 style), covering TLS termination and the server state behind `jti` tracking and refresh-token bindings. Left for -01.

pulls.title: Fresh-eyes review fixes: error precedence, required binding, grant definition, open issues
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Fixes from the fresh-eyes review of main (9d084f5), by a working-group reviewer and an implementer reading cold. There is one commit per finding, so any of them can be dropped on its own.

## Commits

| # | Finding | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Open issues | The grant-type question moves to the top, and four issues are added: an unbound grant after a binding request, refresh-token binding for confidential clients, strict confirmation-member rules, and `jwk` acceptance. This is the author's edit to Appendix B, committed exactly as written. |
| 1 | §5.5 contradicted RFC 7523 §3.1, which says the error for an invalid JWT "MUST be the "invalid_grant" error code" | `invalid_client` now applies only when there is no client authentication and the grant passes every check but has no `cnf` claim. An invalid grant gets the error code of the check it fails. The "unless … `invalid_client`" clause in §5.2 is removed. |
| 2 | Nothing covered a profile that requires binding when the request is not a binding request | §4.2.4: if the profile requires binding and the issuer does not bind, it MUST NOT issue the grant, and in response to a Token Exchange request it MUST return `invalid_target`. The rule moves out of §4.2.1. Other issuance interfaces (§4.5) inherit the prohibition but not the Token Exchange error code. Open issue 2 is updated to match. |
| 3 | "A JWT whose `aud` claim identifies an authorization server" is not something an issuer can check | A grant is now defined by what the issuer issues it for. The issuer decides this from `requested_token_type` (§8, item 1) and from its configuration for `audience` and `resource`. |
| 4 | A subject token and actor token bound to different DPoP keys | §4.2.3 now says that RFC 9449 §4.3 allows only one DPoP header. Such a request is rejected unless the audience exemption covers each token whose key the proof does not match; the existing MUST already required that. |
| 5 | A client registered only for `jwt-dpop`, at a server that advertises both grant types, matched neither SHOULD | The `jwt-dpop` SHOULD becomes "Otherwise", conditioned on the client's registration, and its rationale now covers that case. |
| 6 | The `cnf` response parameter was REQUIRED for every bound token from Token Exchange, which added requirements to access-token responses whose binding RFC 9449 and RFC 8705 govern | It is now REQUIRED only when `token_type` is `N_A`, and still MUST NOT be present for an unbound token. Commit 14 corrects the rule for other bound tokens. |
| 7 | §3.1 read as requiring every server to accept `jwk` | Accepting `jwk` is now MAY, and §1 is aligned. The §3.1 rejection rule now reads "unless the claim contains exactly one confirmation member and the resource authorization server supports that member's confirmation method". Open issue 9 now says "can also accept". |
| 8 | Error precedence was only partly defined | §6 gets one ordered list. It starts with failed client authentication (only when the request includes client authentication), then `unauthorized_client` for an authenticated client, then DPoP errors, then the per-role codes. At the resource authorization server the order is `invalid_grant`, then `unauthorized_client` for a client identified from the grant, then `invalid_client`. |
| 9 | RFC 7591 and RFC 9201 are relied on normatively | Both move to the normative references. Both are Proposed Standards, so neither is a downref. |
| 10 | Requirements written in lowercase | §3.1 now says "The `cnf` claim of a grant that an issuing authorization server binds MUST contain exactly one of these members"; §4.2 now says "MUST support the `cnf` response parameter … MUST NOT bind a grant other than as described". |
| 11 | The §4.2.3 audience exemption with a shared `aud` | §9 (Theft of the Subject Token) now describes how far the exemption reaches: every authenticated client, other than the one the token was issued to, that the issuer associates with the token's `aud` or its records. No requirement is added. |
| 12 | Metadata fetch failure | Metadata that cannot be retrieved or validated is no evidence of any confirmation method. The `jwt-dpop` evidence sentence now refers to metadata "retrieved and validated as described above". |
| 13 | IANA collision | Open issue 5 notes that JWT-DPOP-GRANT §9.1 also requests the `jwt-dpop` registration. |
| 14 | Review of 3301f6e: commit 6 made `cnf` OPTIONAL for every non-`N_A` bound token, including a `pop` token with a symmetric key, where RFC 9201 §3.2 makes it "REQUIRED if the token type is "pop" and a symmetric key is used" | For a bound token whose `token_type` is not `N_A`, `cnf` is now OPTIONAL unless another specification requires it, citing RFC 9201 §3.2. Narrowing the REQUIRED to `N_A` is a design choice: RFC 9201's permission to omit `cnf` for asymmetric keys would not have stopped this document from requiring it. |

## Evidence

- **Build:** each commit built when it was applied. The draft is now 40 pages, up from 38, with no artwork line over 72 columns and no uncited references. The idnits warning (3 × `SECTION_TITLE_HAS_UNEXPECTED_INDENTATION`) is the same on main.
- **BCP 14 sentences:** 48 before, 54 after; keywords 54 before, 61 after.
- **Removed sentences** (normative diff against main), each intended:
  - the old §5.5 MUST and its precedence sentence (commit 1);
  - the "unless {{client-auth}} requires `invalid_client`" mapping in §5.2 (commit 1);
  - the §4.2.1 `invalid_target` MUST, which moved to §4.2.4 as a MUST NOT that covers every request, plus a Token Exchange MUST for the error code (commit 2);
  - the earlier wordings of the `cnf` REQUIRED (commits 6 and 14), the `jwt-dpop` SHOULD (commit 5), and the `jwt-dpop` metadata MAY (commit 12).
- **Added:**
  - the MAY for `jwk`;
  - the two issuer MUSTs;
  - the MUST NOT for a required binding;
  - the precedence MUST and its five list items;
  - the new §5.5 MUST and its error mapping.
- **Paragraph leads:** three keyword sentences now open a paragraph. Two were already the openers in lowercase (§3.1 and §4.2), and the third, the precedence list, scopes itself.

## Cold check of the fix commits

A reader with no session context checked the 13 fix commits against the surrounding text and RFC 9449, 6749, and 7523. All ten defects it found are fixed in the commits above. Two of them undid parts of the round's own fixes:
- The first precedence item had read "`invalid_client`, if client authentication fails". RFC 6749 §5.2 counts "no client authentication included" as a failure, so that put `invalid_client` back ahead of `invalid_grant`.
- The moved `invalid_target` rule had dropped its MUST.

Apart from that first item, the reader found no conflict between the error order and the RFCs: RFC 9449 §5 and §8 and RFC 7523 §3.1 and §3.2 do not order their error codes against each other.

## Not in this PR

These came up in the review and are still open:
- §4.4 "SHOULD treat the response as an error" → MUST discard;
- what counts as a bound subject token when `cnf` has unknown members;
- the Figure 16 lead-in;
- the three design challenges:
  - three grant types for one request format;
  - the client deciding whether to bind;
  - merging with JWT-DPOP-GRANT, with its author as co-author.

pulls.title: Editorial polish (no normative change)
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
An editorial polish of main (f186611). No requirement changes. Each commit is one kind of fix, so any of them can be dropped on its own.

## Commits

| # | Change |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Referents.** These named the wrong thing: a certificate called a "request", a request at the resource authorization server "for" a grant it presents, a Token Exchange request "bound to a certificate", a "therefore" in §4.2.3 that didn't follow from the previous sentence, "The check" with no antecedent, "its key or certificate" with two possible antecedents, and the single-use pointer aimed at §4 instead of §4.2. The Grant Type Substitution note now also covers a server that doesn't accept `jwk`, to match processing item 1. |
| 2 | **Method, not member.** `jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported` lists confirmation methods. Three sentences called them confirmation members. |
| 3 | **Long sentences.** Reworded in §4 (the sources for deciding that a token is a grant), §4.2.1, §4.2.2, §5.1 (the reason for preferring `jwt-dpop` is now its own sentence), §5.5 (the error code comes before the long object, and the stray comma is gone here and in §6) and §7.2 (two sentences that said the same thing are now one). |
| 4 | **Paragraphs.** §3.1 now says "exactly one" only in the MUST, and the resource authorization server's rules get their own paragraph. §5.4 and Theft of the Subject Token are split by topic. |
| 5 | **Example lead-ins.** Figure 2 opens with "The following is an example of" like the others. Figure 5's lead-in puts the audience before the client's authentication method. Figure 14's lead-in now ends at the figure. Figure 16's lead-in now says why the client adds a DPoP proof (it obtained the refresh token with both proofs), and the text after Figure 17 says what the DPoP proof is checked against. |
| 6 | **Openers and wording.** §5 and §7 each get a one-sentence opener, as §3 has. Smaller wording fixes in the abstract, the introduction, §1.1, §9.4, §10, §11.1 and Appendix A. §1.1 no longer starts a rendered line with "Appendix A", which removes one idnits warning. |

## Evidence

- **No normative change:** after every commit, the ordered sequence of BCP 14 keywords matches main (60), and so do the 19 fenced blocks and every anchor.
- **Keyword sentences reworded** (each one intended): the metadata MAY in §7.1 ("method" instead of "member"), the §4.2.1 MUST (one `{{bind}}` pointer dropped), the `jwt-dpop` SHOULD (its "because" clause split off), and the §5.5 MUST (clauses reordered). One sentence that maps a condition to an error code was reworded from "A request for a DPoP-bound grant that carries no DPoP proof" to "A request that presents a DPoP-bound grant without a DPoP proof", with the same scope.
- **Paragraph leads:** the `jwk` MAY now opens its own paragraph. It had no condition to lose.
- **Build:** 42 pages, up from 40 because the text grew by 185 words (1.8%). No artwork line is over 72 columns, and no reference is unresolved or uncited. idnits drops from three `SECTION_TITLE_HAS_UNEXPECTED_INDENTATION` warnings to two. Both remaining ones are the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices.

## Cold check

A reader with no session context checked each hunk against a record of every keyword sentence taken before the pass, which keeps each sentence with its previous sentence and paragraph lead. It found no change to any condition, keyword or error mapping. It found seven wording problems in the pass's own edits, and each fix is folded into its commit:
- The Grant Type Substitution note had dropped the fixed set of three accepted members.
- In Figure 16's lead-in, "which" attached to the wrong figure, and "the same key" had nothing earlier to refer to.
- The reason after Figure 17 was circular.
- Four readability fixes: Figure 14's colon, the passive sentence in §1.1, "Otherwise" in §4.2.2, and the reason in §5.1, which had lost its "because" and used an ambiguous "may not".

## Not in this PR

These would change requirements:
- §4.4: "SHOULD treat the response as an error" becomes "MUST discard";
- what counts as a bound subject token when `cnf` has unknown members;
- the open issues in Appendix B.

pulls.title: Issuer error codes, issuer-required binding, and same-key rule for bound tokens
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Three changes to the issuing authorization server, from the author's review of main (ee407af): - the issuer's error codes were buried in three subsections; - the issuer could not require binding by its own policy; - the rule that a bound subject or actor token is proven with its own key or certificate sat only in Section 4.2.3. There is one commit per change, so each can be dropped on its own. ## Commits | # | Change | Normative effect | |---|---|---| | 1 | Section 4.2 now opens with an ordered list of the issuer's checks, each naming its error code, as Section 5.2 does for the resource authorization server: (1) the DPoP proof is valid, (2) each bound `subject_token` and `actor_token` is proven or exempt, (3) a required binding is applied. Sections 4.2.1, 4.2.3 and 4.2.4 keep the definitions and binding rules, and Section 6 points to the list items. | None. Three MUSTs move into the list. The 4.2.4 MUST NOT against issuing an unbound grant stays where it is, because Section 4.5 applies it to other issuance interfaces. | | 2 | Binding is required if the profile requires it **or the issuer requires it by policy or by the client's registration** (new MAY). When binding is required and the issuer does not bind the grant, it returns:
• `invalid_dpop_proof` if the request has no DPoP proof and a DPoP proof would let it bind the grant, optionally with a `DPoP-Nonce` header;
• `invalid_request` if the request has neither proof and only a TLS client certificate would let it bind the grant;
• `invalid_target` in every other case. | New: the issuer MAY require binding, MAY send a nonce with the challenge, and returns different error codes. Before, every required-but-unbound case returned `invalid_target`, including a request that simply lacked a proof. | | 3 | Section 4.1 now states, for the client, that a bound `subject_token` or `actor_token` MUST be proven with **the same key or certificate it is bound to**. Because a request carries one DPoP proof, two tokens bound to different DPoP keys cannot both be proven, and a bound grant shares the key of each DPoP-bound token that the request proves. The two sentences that said this in Section 4.2.3 move here. | One client MUST, which mirrors the issuer's existing check (item 2). No new constraint: a certificate-bound subject token proven over mutual TLS in a binding request still yields a grant bound to the DPoP key. | ## Why these error codes The table compares them with what a resource server returns (RFC 9449 §7.1, RFC 8705 §3). The one real difference is a missing proof. A resource server answers it with a `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP` challenge and no error code. A token endpoint must return an `error` (RFC 6749 §5.2), and the closest DPoP code is `invalid_dpop_proof`: | Condition | Resource server | Issuing AS | |---|---|---| | DPoP proof invalid | `invalid_dpop_proof` | `invalid_dpop_proof` | | Nonce needed | `use_dpop_nonce` | `use_dpop_nonce` | | Bound token not proven | `invalid_token` | `invalid_request` (RFC 8693 §2.2.2 requires it for an invalid or unacceptable subject or actor token) | | DPoP required, no proof sent | 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP` challenge | `invalid_dpop_proof`, optionally with `DPoP-Nonce` | | Certificate required, none sent | none specific (RFC 8705 has no certificate-specific code) | `invalid_request` | | Binding not possible for the audience | n/a | `invalid_target` | The missing-proof codes apply only when the issuer can bind the grant with the method that the missing proof would use, as Section 4.2 defines "can bind". Every other required-but-unbound case gets `invalid_target`, so a client is not told to add a proof that would then fail with `invalid_target`. The three cases exclude each other, so the Section 6 precedence list needs no change. A requirement for binding does not override the Section 4.2.2 SHOULD NOT on certificate binding. It also does not make binding required at the resource authorization server, which still reads only the profile (Sections 5.2 and 8). RFC 9449 §5 defines `invalid_dpop_proof` for an *invalid* proof. JWT-DPOP-GRANT uses it for a missing proof, but at the server that redeems the grant, where this draft returns `invalid_grant`. Open issue 2 now asks the working group whether using it for a missing proof at the issuer is acceptable, or whether a new error code should signal that proof of possession is required. Such a code would also tell the case apart from item 2's `invalid_request`. Open issue 6 keeps only the client-side "bind or fail" question. The §1.1 bullet now says that `invalid_grant` for a missing proof applies at the resource authorization server. ## Evidence - **Keywords:** MUST 36 → 36 and MAY 6 → 8. The two new MAYs let the issuer require binding and send a `DPoP-Nonce` with the challenge. - Commit 1 replaces three MUSTs with the MUSTs of the list's opening sentence. - Commit 3 adds the client MUST. - **Paragraph leads:** two keyword sentences now open a paragraph: the list's opening sentence and the §4.1 client MUST. Each carries its condition in the sentence ("For a Token Exchange request for a JWT authorization grant", "If the `subject_token` or `actor_token` is bound"). - **Examples:** one new example, the `invalid_dpop_proof` challenge with `DPoP-Nonce`. The `invalid_target` example's description now reads "Audience does not accept DPoP-bound grants". No other code block changed. - **Build:** 44 pages, up from 42 (+687 words). No artwork line is over 72 columns, and every reference is cited. idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices. - **Cold check:** - A reader with no session context confirmed that commit 1 moves its three MUSTs with the same party, condition, behavior and error code. - It worked through five required-binding requests against item 3, and checked the claims about RFC 9449 §7.1 and §8.2, RFC 8693 §2.2.2 and JWT-DPOP-GRANT. - It found 12 defects in the first version, and all are fixed: - item 1 and item 3 read as "if not X"; - "could bind" was undefined when the request carries no proof; - the §6 definitions were wider than item 3; - an inaccurate RFC 9449 §7.1 analogy; - JWT-DPOP-GRANT's use of `invalid_dpop_proof` was attributed to the wrong server; - the `invalid_target` example's description was too broad; - issuer policy had leaked into the §8 profile defaults; - two stale cross-references in Security and Privacy Considerations; - three wording ambiguities. - A second pass on the fix diff confirmed all 12 fixed. It found one new problem: the "can bind" sentence read as a permission rather than a definition. It also found two overclaims in commit 2's message. All are fixed. ## Not in this PR - §4.4 "SHOULD treat the response as an error" becomes "MUST discard". - What counts as a bound subject token when `cnf` has unknown members. ## Review follow-up (commit 4) A review of 3ae320f found that "can bind" checked only that the issuer supports a method and that the audience verifies it. It did not check whether the grant's profile or the issuer's policy permits the method. Under a certificate-only profile where both servers support both methods, a request with neither proof received `invalid_dpop_proof`, and the certificate challenge could never be reached. "Can bind" now also requires that the profile of the grant and the issuer's policy permit the method. Section 4.2.2's separate certificate check is unchanged: the profile requires certificate binding, or the client's registration says it presents the certificate. The same eligibility rule now governs: - the §4.2.1 MUST that binds a binding request to the DPoP key. Before, it applied even under a profile that forbids `jkt`; - the §4.2.2 MAY that binds to the TLS client certificate. Scenarios checked: | Profile | Request | Result | |---|---|---| | certificate-only, binding required | neither proof | `invalid_request` (certificate challenge) | | certificate-only | DPoP proof | unbound grant, or `invalid_target` if binding is required | | DPoP-only, binding required | TLS client certificate only | `invalid_dpop_proof`; no certificate binding | Keyword sequence unchanged; no paragraph gains a keyword-led opening; build passes.

pulls.title: Drop the issuer's audience-verification precondition for binding
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Removes the requirement that an issuing authorization server determine, before binding, that every server in the grant's audience verifies the binding. The resource authorization server enforces the binding, and errors from configuration drift surface there.

## Why

Without the precondition, a bound grant is never *less protected against theft* than an unbound one:

| | With the precondition (main) | Without it (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| Resource AS does not verify the binding | unbound grant: bearer | bound grant: still bearer there (RFC 7519 §4, RFC 7800 §3.1) |
| Resource AS does verify, but the issuer's view is stale | unbound: protection lost | bound and enforced |
| `aud` lists several servers and only some verify | unbound everywhere | enforced where verified |

What the precondition did buy was **availability** at a server that processes `cnf` but rejects the grant. Such a server returns `invalid_grant` for a bound grant where an unbound one was accepted:
- a server that supports this specification but not the method;
- an ID-JAG server without the method;
- a server that implements only JWT-DPOP-GRANT, given a `jwt-bearer` request.

This PR accepts those as late errors at the resource authorization server, and §9.1 says so. The only other thing the precondition bought was a `cnf` response parameter that meant "will be enforced". The "Informational Nature" consideration already disclaims that, and configuration drift breaks it anyway.

## Commits

| # | Change | Normative effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Can bind" means the issuer supports the method and the profile and its policy permit it. A valid binding request therefore yields a bound grant whenever the issuer can bind with `jkt`. §4.2.4 says that the resource AS enforces the binding. §7.1 metadata becomes discovery: a client retrieves it for the server it presents the grant to, and an issuer for each `aud`. The retrieval and evidence rules are kept. §9.1 states the residual risks: theft, availability, and the confirmation member reaching a server that doesn't verify it (also in §10). §1.1 lists the departure from JWT-DPOP-GRANT §7.1, which says an issuer SHOULD NOT issue a bound grant unless it knows the server supports it. **ID-JAG conflict 1 is resolved** and removed from Appendix A, and open issue 5 now counts two. | Removed: the §4.2.4 MUST NOT and the two §7.1 MAYs that let an issuer rely on metadata. Through "can bind", the §4.2.1 MUST and §4.2.2 MAY now apply whenever the method is supported and permitted. |
| 2 | **Optional, droppable.** The issuer's policy can decline a method that it has determined (from configuration, a trust relationship, or metadata) the audience does not verify. That method is then one it "cannot bind" with, so §4.2.1, §4.2.2 and item 3 apply as they do to an unsupported method. §7.1 gains negative evidence: an omission from `jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported` means "not verified", unless `jwt-dpop` says otherwise for `jkt`. Appendix A.1 says that ID-JAG's IdP does not decline `jkt`, because ID-JAG -06 §9.11.1.1 binds whenever the proof is valid. | No BCP 14 keyword. It names a reason the existing "policy permits" clause can use. |

**Commit 2's trade-off:** an issuer that uses the option issues an unbound grant to a binding request for such an audience, when binding is not required. That is the removed precondition, now as an issuer's choice that requires positive knowledge instead of a default. It can't avoid the `jwt-bearer` rejection by a server that implements only JWT-DPOP-GRANT, because that server does verify `jkt`. Drop commit 2 to leave every enforcement error to the resource authorization server.

## Evidence

- **Keywords:** removed exactly the §4.2.4 MUST NOT and the two §7.1 MAYs. Nothing is added, and no keyword sentence newly opens a paragraph.
- **Examples:** the `invalid_target` example's description is now "DPoP binding is not permitted for this grant". The metadata example's lead-in no longer describes it as permission to bind.
- **Build:** 44 pages. Every reference resolves and is cited. idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices.

## Cold check

A reader with no session context checked both commits:
- Leftovers: it searched the whole draft for text that still assumed the old check.
- Claims: the security claim, against RFC 7519, RFC 7800, RFC 7523, JWT-DPOP-GRANT and ID-JAG.
- Walks: four cases of required binding against item 3, §4.2.1, §4.2.2, §4.2.4 and the §6 precedence.
- The rewritten §7.1.

It found six defects in the first version, all fixed:
- The security claim held only against theft. The three availability cases and the privacy cost were missing.
- §1.1 didn't list the departure from JWT-DPOP-GRANT §7.1.
- The first commit 2 was a MAY that contradicted the "if, and only if" definition of "can bind" and still forced binding when binding was not required. It was replaced by the policy formulation.
- §7.1 lacked the negative evidence that the option needs.
- §7.1 gave a client the issuer's retrieval rule.
- Ignoring an unknown claim was attributed to RFC 7800, where it belongs to RFC 7519 §4.

A second pass on the fix diff found four more, all fixed:
- §9.1 and both commit messages claimed the option avoids rejection by a server that implements only JWT-DPOP-GRANT, which verifies `jkt`.
- The negative evidence conflicted with the `jwt-dpop` evidence.
- "verifies" became "must verify", to match §8.
- Appendix A.1 now states ID-JAG's constraint on the option.

The two removed MAYs are classified as follows. The first is deliberate: metadata is no longer the issuer's permission to bind. The second is preserved as the plain statement that `jwt-dpop` "is also evidence".

## Review follow-up (commit 3)

A review of 71cb3aa found two gaps in what the draft promised about enforcement. Both are fixed without restoring the precondition, and no requirement changes:

- **Multi-audience grants.** §7.1 had a client check only the server to which it presents the grant. With `aud = [A, B]`, where A verifies the binding and B accepts the grant as a bearer grant, that check passes, but a thief can redeem the grant at B. A client that needs the binding to be enforced now needs evidence for **each** `aud` value, from metadata, configuration, or the profile. A client that cannot read an encrypted grant's `aud` relies on configuration or the profile for the audience.
- **Required binding changes the guarantee.** "Never weaker than issuing the grant unbound" compares binding with the alternative when binding is *optional*. When binding is *required*, main refused to issue a grant whose enforcement could not be established. This PR can issue a bound grant that an audience accepts as a bearer grant. §9.1 now states this deliberate change: a requirement for binding ensures that the grant is bound, not that the binding is enforced. Where enforcement is needed, it comes from the profile, from configuration that restricts the audience, or from the issuer's policy. New **open issue 10** asks the working group whether a required binding should also require that determination.

Commit 3 doesn't touch the sentence that commit 2 adds, so commit 2 remains droppable. The keyword sequence is identical, and no code block changes.

pulls.title: Explain why the DPoP proof, not the TLS certificate, selects the grant's key
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Explains why a grant issued in response to a binding request is bound only to the key of the DPoP proof, never to a TLS client certificate that the same request presents. Section 4.2.1 states the rule and Appendix A asks ID-JAG to adopt it, but neither said why. No requirement changes. One commit per change, so each can be dropped on its own. ## Commits | # | Change | |---|---| | 1 | **Rationale.** There are two reasons:
• *Contract:* the DPoP proof selects the grant's key, and the certificate serves only for client authentication (§4.1). A client can authenticate to the issuer with a certificate that it doesn't use downstream; binding to that certificate could produce a grant it cannot redeem.
• *Replay:* a DPoP proof covers neither the TLS connection nor the request. An attacker who captures a request that proves possession of a DPoP-bound `subject_token` or `actor_token` can replay both over its own mutual-TLS connection. A grant bound to the attacker's certificate would be usable; one bound to the DPoP key is not.
§9.4 already made the replay argument for the resource authorization server; it now also covers the issuer. For a bearer `subject_token` the choice adds no protection, because a thief can already request a grant bound to its own key. §4.2.1 and the Appendix A bullet now give both reasons. "Theft of the Subject Token" gets the anchor `subject-token-theft`. | | 2 | **Open question (droppable).** The rule is broader than its security reason requires: the replay case needs a DPoP-bound input token. Open issue 4 now also asks whether a client's certificate opt-in should allow a certificate binding alongside a DPoP proof, except when the request proves possession of a DPoP-bound token, as ID-JAG §9.11 leaves to policy. That would resolve the certificate conflict with ID-JAG, but the client's check in §4.4 would then also have to accept the certificate. Appendix A points to the question. | ## Evidence - **Keywords:** the ordered sequence is identical to main (59), and no keyword sentence was removed, added, or newly opens a paragraph. - **Code blocks:** the 20 fenced blocks are unchanged. - **Build:** 45 pages. Every reference is cited. idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices. - **Build:** 46 pages after commits 3 and 4, with the same results. - **Cold check:** a reader with no session context checked the replay argument against RFC 9449, the description of ID-JAG §9.11, and the open-issue alternative. It confirmed the core argument and the ID-JAG description, and found seven defects. Commits 3 and 4 fix them, one for each original commit, so commit 2 and its fix can still be dropped together: - §4.2.1: the certificate also proves possession of a certificate-bound subject or actor token, so it does not serve "only for client authentication". - §9.4: the opening "The same applies" could be read as extending the resource authorization server's `jti` SHOULD to the issuer. - §9.4: the attacker's client-authentication condition was incomplete. Authenticating as its own client (RFC 9449 §11.11) defeats even mutual-TLS client authentication, and "as for a public client" was the weakest example. - §9.4: an unbound grant was a missing third outcome that the attacker can use. - Open issue 4 said the alternative would "resolve" the ID-JAG conflict; it would only narrow it. It also listed only the §4.4 change, when exceptions to §4.1, §4.2.1, §4.2.2 and item 3 are also needed. - Two errors in the original commit messages: the RFC 9449 section is §11.7, not §4.3, and "resolve" should read "narrow". The follow-up commit messages record both corrections instead of a force-push. ## Review follow-up (commit 5) A review of 6ed13ea found two overstatements in the new §9.4 text, both fixed. No requirement changes: - **"Of no use to the attacker"** now holds only at a resource authorization server that verifies the binding. Since PR #7, a bound grant can be issued for an audience that ignores the binding, where the attacker can redeem it as a bearer grant (§9.1). A grant bound to the attacker's certificate would be usable at every server in its audience. - **"No protection for a bearer `subject_token`"** was too broad. With a bearer subject token and an actor token bound to K, the attacker cannot substitute its own DPoP key, so keeping the grant bound to K still blocks the certificate rebinding. The exception now applies only when **neither** input token requires proof of possession of a DPoP key. - Appendix A now names the `actor_token` in the replay reason, as §4.2.1 does.

pulls.title: Clarify refresh proofs, required vs enforced binding, and profile acceptance rules
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Targeted clarifications from a re-assessed external review. The review's test was the smallest change that resolves an observed problem. Commits 1 to 5 change no requirement; commit 6 changes one, and can be dropped on its own.

## Commits

| # | Change | Normative effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Refresh proofs (§5.4).** A client that already knows a refresh token's binding, from the profile or its configuration at the resource authorization server, presents only the proof that the binding needs, and none for a refresh token bound only to the client. It need not keep another key or certificate for that refresh token, though a certificate it uses for client authentication stays needed. A client that doesn't know the binding still presents every proof. | None. The instruction was already lowercase, and no response field is added. |
| 2 | **Public clients and Table 2 (§5.3).** RFC 9449 §5 requires a refresh token issued to a public client that presents a valid DPoP proof to be bound to that key. §5.3 inherits that rule and only narrows it, so for a certificate-bound grant with both proofs the result is the DPoP key. A sentence under the table now says so. It is scoped to "a narrower binding", so it doesn't reinstate RFC 9449's binding to the client for confidential clients, which §5.4 deliberately overrides. | None. |
| 3 | **Required ≠ enforced (§4.2, §8 item 3).** Where "binding is required" is defined, §4.2 now says that a required binding is applied, not that every audience enforces it, and points to §9.1. Profile item 3 asks a profile that promises enforcement to say who establishes that the audience verifies the binding, and from what evidence. Open issue 10 keeps the question of whether the default should change. | None. |
| 4 | **Bind or fail (§4.1, open issue 6).** §4.1 now tells a client that always needs binding that it can establish this through the profile or its registration at the issuer; §4.2 already makes the issuer bind or reject in that case. Open issue 6 is narrowed to whether a per-request option is needed for a requirement that neither the profile nor the registration expresses. | None. |
| 5 | **Cross-endpoint replay (§9.4).** "A DPoP proof sent to one cannot be replayed at the other" now applies only when the two token endpoints differ. | None. |
| 6 | **Profile acceptance rules (§8 item 1, §9.3).** RFC 8725 §3.12 requires mutually exclusive validation rules, and explicit typing is one way to get them. Profile item 1 now asks for the rules that distinguish the grant from other JWTs, including the `typ` value and whether the rules rely on it. §9.3 keeps its SHOULD to reject a grant without the profile's `typ`, and adds a **MUST** where the profile relies on `typ` to distinguish its grants. | One new MUST, conditioned on the profile. |

## Not in this PR

- **"Replaces" / "legacy" wording:** held until the author has discussed a combined draft with the author of JWT-DPOP-GRANT.
- **Deferred until a use case is established:** a field in the refresh response that signals the binding, changing the grant's key to one other than the proof's (as in ID-CHAINING's `requested_cnf`), and a negotiation parameter for issuance.
- **No change:** `jwt-pop`, because open issue 1 already presents it as a trade-off, and the precedence in §6, because no ordering defect was shown.

## Evidence

- **Keywords:** through commit 5 the ordered keyword sequence is identical to main (59), and all 20 code blocks are unchanged. Commit 6 changes only the `typ` sentence in §9.3. No keyword sentence newly opens a paragraph.
- **Build:** 47 pages. Every reference is cited. idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices.
- **Build:** 48 pages after commits 7 and 8, with the same results. Across the PR, the only keyword change is commit 6's MUST.
- **Cold check:** a reader with no session context checked every commit against RFC 9449, RFC 8725, ID-JAG and the draft's own rules. Commit 5 was accurate. It found five defects in the draft text and three in commit messages, all fixed: commit 7 for commits 1 to 4, and commit 8 for commit 6, so commits 6 and 8 can still be dropped together.
  - **Commit 1 could make a client fail.** A client registered with `dpop_bound_access_tokens` must send a DPoP proof (RFC 9449 §5.2), and without the proof it gets certificate-bound or Bearer tokens instead of DPoP-bound ones. It also cannot see the resource authorization server's configuration. The text now lets a client omit only a proof that the binding doesn't need, when the profile or an arrangement establishes the binding. It keeps the DPoP proof wherever the client's registration requires one or the client needs DPoP-bound tokens.
  - **Commit 2's general "narrower binding" clause reinstated RFC 9449's rule for confidential clients.** That rule narrows row 3 to the certificate, contradicting §5.4 and the refresh example. The note now applies only to public clients, and says the confidential-client statement does not apply.
  - **Commit 4 overclaimed.** A client cannot make a profile require binding, and no client metadata records the requirement. The text now says the client requests a grant whose profile requires binding, or arranges this with the issuer.
  - **Commit 3:** item 3 lets the issuer reject instead of binding, so the wording is now "ensures that an issued grant is bound".
  - **Commit 6:** the RFC 8725 §3.12 citation now covers only JWTs from the same issuer. The MUST now applies when the profile *states* that it relies on `typ`, which a resource authorization server can check. Appendix A.1 now says ID-JAG relies on `typ` (ID-JAG §4.4.1).
  - §9.1 now cites profile items 2 and 3.
  - The commit 7 and 8 messages record the corrections to the earlier commit messages, instead of a force-push.

## Review follow-up (commit 9)

A review of 147d7c7 found that commit 5's condition, "when their token endpoints differ", still overstated the protection. A token endpoint URI can include a query component (RFC 6749 §3.2), and RFC 9449 §4.3 compares `htu` with the request URI "ignoring any query and fragment parts". So `/token?role=issuer` and `/token?role=resource` on the same origin share an `htu`, and one proof passes the URI check at both. The condition is now that the two token endpoint URIs don't match under RFC 9449 §4.3's comparison, and the text names the query-only case. No requirement changes.

pulls.title: Use "key-bound authorization grant" and "authorization grant" throughout
pulls.author: mcguinness

pulls.title: Readability pass: simpler sentences, scannable lists, fewer repeated references
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
A readability, scannability, and approachability pass. It simplifies language, reduces density, and removes cross-references that repeat. **No requirement changes.** There is one commit per section group, so any of them can be dropped on its own. ## Commits | # | Scope | Main changes | |---|---|---| | 1 | Abstract, §1, §1.1 | • Abstract: three sentences instead of one.
• Bearer-token problem stated plainly.
• Roadmap as a list.
• §1.1 uses the short grant-type names. | | 2 | §4 | • §4: the scope paragraph is split.
• §4.1: the bound-token MUST lists its two consequences.
• §4.2: "binding is required" is split from the definition of "can bind"; item 3's bullets are shorter.
• §4.2.1: the requirements and the rationale are separate paragraphs, and the two reasons are a list.
• §4.2.2 and §4.2.4: shorter wording. | | 3 | §5 | • §5.1 and §5.1.2: short grant-type names; the subject of the §5.1.2 processing sentence is explicit.
• §5.4: the binding rule and the timing of its exception are separate paragraphs; the "which proofs to present" paragraph is split; the example lead-in is three short sentences. | | 4 | §7 | • §7.1: who retrieves which metadata is a list by role; the evidence rules are a list.
• §7.2: the first paragraph is split. | | 5 | §9 | • §9.1: four paragraphs become three; the costs of binding are a list.
• §9.2: what `jwt-pop` adds is a list.
• §9.4: the cross-endpoint paragraph is shorter; the issuer replay paragraph is split into conditions, a list of outcomes, and the exception.
• §9.8: the exemption paragraph is split into sentences. | | 6 | Whole document | Drops 13 parenthetical cross-references that repeat within a subsection or point to the subsection the reader is in. It keeps citations attached to an identifier (such as an error code and the section that defines it), citations of other documents inside keyword sentences, inline references, citations listing several sources, everything in Open Issues, and two repeats that name the rule being applied. | Not changed: the examples, the diagram, the IANA section, the open issues, and the Appendix A text. ## Measured | | main | this PR | RFC 9449 | |---|---|---|---| | Average sentence (words) | 24.6 | 23.0 | 21.1 | | 90th-percentile sentence | 44 | 41 | 35 | | Words (source) | 13,176 | 13,036 | | | Internal cross-references | 226 | 213 | | The 129 citations of other documents' sections are left in place. Nearly all are first uses that point at the exact rule relied on, and fewer than 30 repeat even within a top-level section, most of them in definitions or keyword sentences. Further cuts are the author's call: cite once per top-level section, or drop citations for imported terms such as "DPoP proof". ## Evidence of no normative change - **Keywords:** the ordered BCP 14 keyword sequence (60) is identical to main. - **Code blocks and anchors:** all 20 fenced blocks and all anchors are unchanged. - **Paragraph leads:** no keyword sentence newly opens a paragraph. - **Build:** 48 pages, every reference cited, and idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices. - **Cold check:** a reader with no session context checked every reworded keyword sentence and rule against a record of each keyword sentence on main, with its previous sentence and paragraph lead. It found 18 defects, each fixed in the commit that introduced it. Six had changed a rule's scope: - §5.1.2 said `jwt-dpop` requests are processed "as a `jwt-pop` request", which points at a grant type the server may not support. - In §9.1, an added "only" reversed an implication. - §9.1's JWT-DPOP-GRANT bullet had widened from DPoP-bound grants to all grants. - In §9.1, "it" referred to the wrong server. - In §7.1, "do so" attached to the wrong verb. - In §7.1, "configuration can still provide that evidence" had come loose from one of its two cases. The other twelve were dropped qualifiers, two citations that carried meaning, and pronouns made ambiguous by splitting. A second pass confirmed all 18 fixed. It found two reference problems in the reader's own suggested wording, also fixed. ## Review follow-up (commit 7) A review of 2e0a929 found no processing-rule regressions. It noted one overstatement. In the introduction, "These grants are bearer tokens" followed a sentence naming both identity chaining and ID-JAG, so it also covered ID-JAG grants, which ID-JAG §9.11 already lets the issuer bind with DPoP or a certificate. The previous wording attributed the statement to ID-CHAINING alone. It now reads "Without a proof-of-possession binding, these grants are bearer tokens". No requirement changes.

pulls.title: Delegate restatements of dependency specs and cut repeated points
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Removes text that restates dependency specifications, or that repeats a point this document makes elsewhere. **No requirement changes.** One commit per change, so any of them can be dropped on its own.

## Commits

| # | Where | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | §5.2 | Drops "validates a DPoP proof … before it validates the authorization grant, and rejects an invalid proof as RFC 9449 Section 5 requires". RFC 9449 §5 and the §6 error order already cover it. **Kept:** the next sentence ("… rejected with `invalid_grant` (item 2), not `use_dpop_nonce`"). It is load-bearing: a request with no proof also has no nonce, and §6 ranks `use_dpop_nonce` first. |
| 2 | §5.2 | Drops the TLS-terminating-proxy scope note, which restates RFC 8705 §6.5. **Kept:** that the server need not authenticate the client with the certificate or trust its issuer, which tells an implementer what it can skip. |
| 3 | §9.5 → §9.6 | Folds "Replay by the Key Holder", which restated RFC 7523 and ID-CHAINING §5.5, into "Exhaustion of Single-Use Authorization Grants" as one opening sentence. Nothing linked to the removed heading. |
| 4 | §9.7 | "Proof of Possession and Client Identity" states the RFC 9449 §11.11 fact in one clause, then its consequence for a grant in place of client authentication. |
| 5 | §4.4 | The `token_type` behavior of RFC 9449 and RFC 8705 in one sentence instead of two. |
| 6 | §6 | The `use_dpop_nonce` definition points to RFC 9449 §8 instead of restating its conditions, and keeps the MUST narrowing. The `invalid_dpop_proof` definition already points to RFC 9449 and is unchanged. |
| 7 | §3.2 | Drops the "JSON member order and insignificant whitespace are ignored" bullet, which "compared by confirmation method and value, not by byte representation" already implies. |
| 8 | Open issue 1 | Points to §9.2 for the contrast between rejecting an unsupported grant type and ignoring unknown client metadata. Keeps the one point §9.2 doesn't make: a client could check registered metadata (RFC 7591 §3.2.1). The question is unchanged. |

## Not in this PR

These change requirements or are the author's call:
- Moving the ID-JAG conflict analysis in Appendix A to the repository.
- Dropping `jwk` acceptance (open issue 9).
- Narrowing the `cnf` response parameter to `N_A` grants (open issue 3).
- Dropping the issuer's "decline a method" option.
- Dropping the legacy `jwt-dpop` grant type.

## Evidence

- **Keywords:** the ordered BCP 14 keyword sequence (60) is identical to main. The only reworded keyword sentence is the `use_dpop_nonce` MUST, where "these conditions" became "those conditions" with the same antecedent.
- **Code blocks and anchors:** all 20 fenced blocks and all anchors are unchanged. No keyword sentence newly opens a paragraph.
- **Build:** 47 pages, down from 48 (−166 words). Every reference is cited. idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices.
- **Net change:** −137 words after commits 9–11.
- **Cold check:** a reader with no session context checked each removal against the cached dependency text. Commits 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 are clean. Three defects were found and are fixed by commits 9–11, each correcting one earlier commit:
  - **Commit 1** removed the only statement that a resource authorization server rejects an invalid DPoP proof whatever the grant's binding. §5.2 names `invalid_dpop_proof` only for DPoP-bound grants, so an invalid proof sent with an unbound or certificate-bound grant had no named outcome. Commit 9 restores the rule in short form, with its RFC 9449 pointer.
  - **Commit 6's** `use_dpop_nonce` definition, "the conditions for which RFC 9449 Section 8 defines this error code", literally covered a request with no DPoP proof. That contradicted §5.2's `invalid_grant` rule and item 3 of §4.2. Commit 11 limits the definition to a request that contains a DPoP proof, as main assumed. The keyword sentence now reads "for such a proof", with the same scope as main.
  - **Commit 5** dropped "of `DPoP`", so it read as if every access token's `token_type` shows a DPoP binding. Commit 10 restores the condition.
- **Keywords and blocks:** the keyword sequence and all fenced blocks are still identical to main.

pulls.title: Drop Section X links that only signpost or repeat
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Removes "Section X" links that only signpost, or that repeat a citation already given in the same section. **No requirement changes.** Two commits, so either can be dropped on its own.

I reviewed all 165 parenthetical links one at a time. 21 are removed; the rest point at something the sentence relies on.

## Commit 1: internal signposts (16, plus one partial)

- Five repeated pointers to the profile list (`{{profiles}}`), after phrases such as "the profile of the grant requires binding".
- Pointers from sentences that already say what the target holds:
  - §4.1 → §5.1 ("the key that it will use to redeem the grant");
  - §4.2.1 → §4.1, §4.4 and §4.2.3;
  - §4.2.4 → §4.2.1 and §4.2.2, after describing the DPoP key and the TLS client certificate;
  - §4.4 → §4.2.4;
  - §5.3 → §5.2 ("which is the key of the DPoP proof");
  - §5.4 → Table 2 (the second pointer to it);
  - §5.5 → §8;
  - §9.1 → §5.2.
- The `{{bind}}` half of the §3.1 citation pair.

## Commit 2: repeated citations of other documents (5)

- RFC 7523 §2.1 in §4, because the Terminology definition of "JWT authorization grant" cites it.
- RFC 8693 §2.2.1 in §4.3, because §4.2.4 cites it.
- RFC 7800 §3.2 for `jwk` in §5.2 item 1, because §3.1 cites it.
- RFC 9449 §4.3 in §5.3, because §5.2 cites it.
- RFC 8705 §2 in the lead-in to the refresh example.

## Kept, by design

- Links in definitions, tables, and the Overview's step list.
- Links to the section that holds the rule or the term a sentence relies on, such as "can bind", "exempt", or the error precedence.
- Links to the reason, in Security Considerations.
- Links attached to an identifier, such as an error code and the section that defines it.
- The first citation of another document in each top-level section, and citations that support a claim about the other document.
- Citations inside BCP 14 keyword sentences.
- Every link used as a noun ("as {{cert-binding}} describes").

## Evidence

- **Keywords:** the ordered BCP 14 keyword sequence (60) is identical to main.
- **Code blocks and anchors:** all 20 fenced blocks and all anchors are unchanged.
- **Paragraph leads:** the only sentence flagged as leading a paragraph is the §5.2 "If the profile … requires binding" MUST, which already opened its paragraph. It lost only its trailing `({{profiles}})`, and its condition is intact.
- **Build:** 47 pages. Every reference is cited. idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices.

pulls.title: Fact-check fixes: citations and ID-JAG description
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Fixes from a fact check of every claim the draft makes about another document. **No requirement changes.** One commit per fix.

## How the check ran

The check covered 174 sentences that cite another document, plus the IANA section. They were checked in four batches against the text of each source, not from memory: section numbers, quotes, names, MUST/SHOULD/MAY strength, and each RFC's status. The four batches were:
- RFC 9449, 7800 and 7638;
- RFC 6749, 7519, 7521, 7523, 7591, 8414, 8725 and 10070;
- RFC 8693, 8705, 9201, 9700, 7516, 6755, plus the IANA registry and its templates;
- ID-JAG, ID-CHAINING, JWT-DPOP-GRANT and TE-CNF, including a datatracker check for newer revisions.

Results:
- **Accuracy:** no wrong section numbers, misquotes, or misspelled names.
- **Revisions:** all four cited drafts are current (ID-JAG -06, ID-CHAINING -17, JWT-DPOP-GRANT -02, TE-CNF -00), and every cited section still exists.
- **Downrefs:** every normative reference is Standards Track. RFC 8725 and RFC 9700 (BCPs) and RFC 6755 (Informational) are cited only informatively, so there is no downref.
- **Registrations:** `jwt-pop`, `jwt-dpop`, and `jwt_grant_cnf_methods_supported` are not yet registered. The `cnf` entry in the OAuth Parameters registry matches the draft's description.

## Commits

| # | Where | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | §5.1 | The client's MUST to send the request over mutual TLS cited RFC 8705 §3. That section's MUST covers requests to a protected resource, not presenting a grant at a token endpoint. The citation is dropped; the requirement is this specification's own. The §5 citation for the endpoint alias stays. |
| 2 | §4.2 | RFC 9449 §8.2 supports supplying a nonce in a DPoP-Nonce header, but not specifically with `invalid_dpop_proof`, so that MAY is this specification's own. "Without an extra round trip" was uncited reasoning. It now says that the repeated request need not first be rejected with `use_dpop_nonce`. |
| 3 | Appendix A.1 | ID-JAG -06 §9.11.1.1 requires `jkt` binding when the DPoP proof is valid "unless it binds the grant to a certificate instead", and §9.11 lets local policy select either. Item 3 said the IdP's policy "does not decline" `jkt`; it now describes the certificate choice and points to the first conflict. The first conflict now says the IdP may "select either a DPoP or a certificate binding". |

## Findings checked and not changed

- **IANA change controller "IESG"** (RFC 8414 §7.1.1's template). Current practice for IETF-stream documents is "IETF": RFC 9449 registered `dpop_signing_alg_values_supported` with "IETF", and the registry holds 8 such entries. The draft's "IETF" matches.
- **The `invalid_target` citation of RFC 8693 §2.2.2** names where the error code is defined; it does not claim that RFC 8693 mandates the code for a binding failure. Open issue 2 already discusses this use.
- **Accurate but loosely worded:**
  - Using `unauthorized_client` for a client identified from the grant extends RFC 6749's "authenticated client". The draft states that extension itself.
  - RFC 8414 §3 includes §3.3, where validation is.
  - RFC 9700 as the reference for protecting bearer subject tokens is loose but acceptable.

## Evidence

- **Keywords:** the ordered BCP 14 keyword sequence (60) is identical to main.
- **Code blocks and anchors:** all fenced blocks and anchors are unchanged.
- **Build:** 47 pages; idnits reports only the two warnings for the table-of-contents lines xml2rfc generates for the appendices.
